claim: SWRBench (the ~1000-PR study) comprises 1000 manually verified GitHub PRs and finds current ACR tools and LLMs underperform; multi-review aggregation boosts F1 by up to 43.67%.
quote: SWRBench... comprising 1000 manually verified Pull Requests (PRs)... systematic evaluation of mainstream ACR tools and LLMs on SWRBench reveals that current systems underperform... increasing F1 scores by up to 43.67%.

claim: On SWRBench the best configuration (PR-Review with Gemini-2.5-Pro) reached an F1 of only 19.38%, with most approaches in the 4.87%-19% range; ground truth was 500 Change-PRs (avg 1.90 change-points) plus 500 Clean-PRs from 12 Python projects, with LLM-judge ~90% human agreement.
quote: the top-performing combination, PR-Review leveraged with Gemini-2.5-Pro, achieved an F1 score of only 19.38%... 500 Change-PRs... 500 Clean-PRs... 12 popular and actively maintained open-source Python projects

claim: CRScore (NAACL 2025) is a reference-free metric grounding code-review-comment evaluation in code claims and smells across conciseness/comprehensiveness/relevance, released with 2.9k human-annotated review quality scores.
quote: CRScore... a reference-free metric to measure dimensions of review quality like conciseness, comprehensiveness, and relevance... released a corpus of 2.9k human-annotated review quality scores

claim: CRScore achieves the highest alignment with human judgment among open-source metrics (Spearman 0.5431) and exposes that reference-based BLEU fails on code review's one-to-many nature, scoring a valid model review as low as 0.0458.
quote: Spearman correlation: 0.5431... a model-generated review may be completely valid yet receive a BLEU score of only 0.0458 due to poor n-gram overlap with the single reference

claim: Microsoft's CodeReviewer (Li et al., 2022) introduced the CodeReview dataset of 7.9M PRs across 9 languages from 1000+ repos, but review-comment generation BLEU stays below 10, indicating an inherently hard task.
quote: CodeReview dataset... containing 7.9 million pull requests... nine most popular languages... CodeReviewer produces a higher BLEU score than the baseline models, though the BLEU score is still lower than 10

claim: CodeReviewQA (2025) reframes evaluation as 900 manually curated multiple-choice cases probing change-type recognition, localization, and solution identification rather than free-text generation.
quote: CodeReviewQA assesses LLM capability beyond text generation using MCQA probes on decomposed reasoning subtasks (change type recognition, localization, and solution identification) across 900 manually curated review cases

claim: A 2026 survey of code review benchmarks reviewed 99 papers (58 pre-LLM, 41 LLM era, 2015-2025), names CodeReviewer/CodeReviewQA/CodeFuse-CR-Bench, and warns benchmarks and metrics remain immature with noisy human-comment ground truth.
quote: 99 papers total: 58 from the Pre-LLM era and 41 from the LLM era, spanning 2015-2025... Most benchmarks treat natural-language human comments as the primary ground truth, which introduces challenges due to noise, incompleteness, and variability

claim: Only 64% of CodeReviewer training comments are valid (~36% noisy), echoing 32% noise in the test set; LLM-based cleaning raises BLEU-4 by 7.5-13% despite 25-66% smaller data.
quote: only 64% of sampled comments in the CodeReviewer training set were valid... approximately 36% were noisy... aligns with prior work showing 32% noise in the test set... BLEU-4 improvements: 7.5% to 13%

claim: A 2026 empirical study of 3,109 AIDev PRs found 12 of 13 code-review agents had average signal ratios below 60% (Copilot 19.79% signal), and CRA-only PRs merged at 45.20% vs 68.37% for human-only review.
quote: 92.31% of CRAs (12 of 13) exhibited average signal ratios below 60%... Copilot at 19.79% signal... CRA-only reviews: 45.20% merge rate... Human-only reviews: 68.37% merge rate

claim: CodeFuse-CR-Bench (Guo et al., 2025) is a comprehensiveness-aware benchmark for end-to-end code review evaluation in Python projects.
quote: CodeFuse-CR-Bench: A Comprehensiveness-aware Benchmark for End-to-End Code Review Evaluation in Python Projects

claim: Greptile's own July 2025 benchmark reports an 82% bug catch rate vs Bugbot 58%, Copilot 54%, CodeRabbit 44%, Graphite 6%, on 50 real bug-fix PRs (10 each) from Sentry, Cal.com, Grafana, Keycloak, Discourse across Python/TypeScript/Go/Java/Ruby, counting a bug 'caught' only when flagged in a line-level comment that explains impact.
quote: Greptile: 82%, Bugbot: 58%, Copilot: 54%, CodeRabbit: 44%, Graphite: 6%. A bug counted as 'caught' only when the tool explicitly identified the faulty code in a line-level comment and explained the impact.

claim: CodeRabbit promotes the independent Martian Code Review Bench (~300,000 PRs over 2 months, Jan-Feb 2026), where it reports the #1 F1 score of 51.2%, precision 49.2%, and the highest recall at 53.5%; Martian uses an 'online' method tracking which comments developers act on plus an 'offline' method of 50 standardized PRs against a gold bug set.
quote: F1 Score: 51.2% (ranked #1 among 10 tools); Precision: 49.2%; Recall: 53.5% (highest of any tool). Dataset: Nearly 300,000 pull requests analyzed over 2 months.

claim: Martian's benchmark (publicized by CodeAnt) evaluated 17 AI code-review tools over 200,000+ real PRs from thousands of repos using an online developer-behavior method (comment counts as true positive when the developer changes code) plus a 50-PR offline set; CodeAnt reports F1 51.7%, precision 52.2%, recall 51.1%, ranking #3.
quote: 200,000+ real pull requests analyzed; 17 AI code review tools evaluated. CodeAnt: F1 51.7%, Precision 52.2%, Recall 51.1%, Global Rank #3. Martian (independent research lab founded by researchers from DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta).

claim: Cursor reports BugBot's proprietary 'resolution rate' (AI determines at merge time which flagged bugs the author actually fixed) rose from 52% to over 70% across 40 major experiments July 2025-Jan 2026, with bugs flagged per run up from 0.4 to 0.7; offline testing uses 'BugBench,' a curated set of real diffs with human-annotated bugs.
quote: Resolution Rate: Increased from 52% to over 70% since launch. BugBench, described as 'a curated benchmark of real code diffs with human annotated bugs' for offline testing. 40 major experiments conducted across versions 1-11.

claim: Qodo's self-built Code Review Benchmark 1.0 (Feb 4, 2026) uses 100 PRs with 580 issues across 7 repos (Redis/C, Tauri/Rust, Dify, ASP.NET Core, etc.) where bugs are LLM-injected by corrupting diffs while preserving functionality plus 1-3 functional bugs each, then double-verified; a 'hit' requires correct description AND correct file/line localization.
quote: 100 PRs containing a total of 580 issues. Compliance violations were introduced using an LLM, 'corrupting the diff while preserving the original functionality.' Hit (True Positive): Tool comment accurately describes the issue AND correctly localizes it to the proper file and line number.

claim: Qodo claims Qodo 2.0 (multi-agent architecture, Feb 2026) leads its own benchmark with the highest F1 at 60.1%, outperforming the next-best tool by 9%, and the highest recall at 56.7%, with competitors showing high precision but extremely low recall.
quote: Qodo 2.0 leads on this benchmark, achieving the highest overall F1 score at 60.1%, outperforming the next best solution by 9% and delivering the highest recall at 56.7%, finding more real issues than any other solution tested.

claim: Bito's own benchmark (updated March 16, 2026) uses a truth set of 65 known issues across TypeScript/Python/JavaScript/Go/Java and reports Bito at 69.5% average coverage, >75% high-severity and >60% medium-severity detection, with CodeRabbit closest at 65.8% and Entelligence, Graphite, Gemini, Copilot, Qodo, CodeAnt lower.
quote: Bito achieved an average coverage of 69.5% across all languages tested. CodeRabbit: 65.8% average coverage (closest competitor). Truth set of 65 known issues across different severities.

claim: Graphite launched its Diamond AI reviewer with a $52M Series B; Diamond optimized for very low false positives but ranked last for bug detection in Martian's benchmark, the name was deprecated 10/08/2025 in favor of Graphite Agent, and Graphite was acquired by Cursor in December 2025 to merge with BugBot.
quote: Graphite raises $52M and launches Diamond to reimagine code review for the age of AI.

claim: Korbit's positioning explicitly argues precision matters most rather than maximizing recall/catch-rate, framing its benchmark narrative around suppressing low-value comments and learning from developer dismissals, a counterpoint to recall-led vendors like Qodo and CodeRabbit.
quote: Korbit was designed with precision and developer trust in mind, ensuring that every flagged issue adds real value to the developer's workflow. Korbit's AI continuously learns from developer feedback.

claim: DeepSource notes that nearly every AI code-review vendor publishes a benchmark in which it ranks first, highlighting that self-constructed datasets, differing 'caught' definitions, and precision-vs-recall framing make cross-vendor numbers non-comparable.
quote: Every AI code review vendor benchmarks itself, and wins.

claim: In Propel's 2026 benchmark, F-scores were led by Propel at 64%, Cursor Bugbot at 49%, and Greptile at 45%, with high-precision agents often paying for it in very low recall.
quote: Propel led with an F-score of 64%, followed by Cursor Bugbot with 49%, and Greptile with 45%

claim: AI code review tools typically achieve false-positive rates in the 5-15% range, with better-tuned tools closer to 5-8%, and balancing signal-to-noise is framed as key to maintaining developer trust.
quote: AI-driven code review systems today typically achieve false-positive rates in the 5–15% range ... a small percentage of incorrect flags is normal, and balancing signal-to-noise is key to maintaining developer trust.

claim: Most vendors design precision-first because distrust and alert fatigue are real, with 46% of developers distrusting AI tool accuracy and 66% citing 'almost right but not quite' as their top frustration; GitHub Copilot, CodeRabbit and Graphite all market on signal/precision.
quote: 46% of developers actively distrust the accuracy of AI tools, and 66% cite 'almost right, but not quite' outputs as their largest frustration.

claim: Practitioners report AI reviewers (CodeRabbit, Codacy) add noise where only a small fraction of comments are useful and can send junior engineers down rabbit holes on non-issues while real bugs go unnoticed.
quote: the AI directs junior engineers into time-wasting rabbit holes around things that are actually non-issues while actual issues with a PR go completely unnoticed

claim: A noisy reviewer erodes trust through a three-stage cycle ending in 'dismiss all', after which true positives get dismissed alongside false ones; at a 15% FPR roughly 13 of 15 'critical' flags per week are false, causing desensitization.
quote: you're paying for a security layer your engineers have learned to ignore, which means true positives get dismissed along with false ones.

claim: The Microsoft study (Bosu, Greiler, Bird 2015) operationally defines a code review comment as useful if it triggers a code change in nearby lines, building a useful/not-useful classifier over 1.5M comments where roughly a third are non-useful.
quote: distinguish between useful and not useful code review feedback ... categorized a total of 1,496,340 review comments from 190,050 review requests across five projects ... 64% to 68% of reviews were classified as useful

claim: The 2025 'Hold On! Is My Feedback Useful?' study adopts the trigger-code-change definition of usefulness and predicts it via four feature aspects (Code, Text, Voice, Jargon), reporting classifier metrics (F1, AUC, MCC) rather than a Likert rubric.
quote: comments are "useful if they trigger code changes" ... Code ... Text ... Voice: Tone, sentiment, toxicity, and empathy indicators ... Jargon ... more than 1 out of 3 CR comments lack utility

claim: Rubric-design guidance stresses concrete behavioral level definitions over vague labels, independently scorable dimensions, 5-7 point Likert or Best-Worst Scaling scales, and validation via Cohen's/Fleiss' kappa and ICC.
quote: Best-Worst Scaling has been shown to yield significantly higher inter-rater reliability than traditional Likert ratings ... Cohen's Kappa, Fleiss' Kappa, and the intraclass correlation coefficient

claim: Golden-dataset guidance recommends defining outcome schemas with rubric scores and rationales, promoting 'silver' synthetic data to 'gold' via human review and evaluator agreement, calibrating annotators through pilot rounds, and measuring inter-annotator agreement before full annotation.
quote: Define outcome schemas with objective fields, rubric scores, and rationales ... Create "silver" synthetic conversations, then promote to "gold" through human review and evaluator agreement checks ... calibrating annotators through "pilot rounds"

claim: Rubric-driven LLM-as-judge frameworks (2026) use explicit well-specified criteria as a bridge between human policy language and machine-checkable rewards, applying Item Response Theory to flag criteria that are too ambiguous or too sensitive.
quote: Rubrics serve as a bridge between human policy language and machine-checkable rewards, allowing the application of Item Response Theory to determine which criteria are too ambiguous or too sensitive

claim: The MT-Bench/Chatbot Arena paper established that strong LLM judges like GPT-4 reach over 80% agreement with human preferences, matching human-to-human agreement, but exhibit position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases plus limited reasoning.
quote: strong LLM judges like GPT-4 can match both controlled and crowdsourced human preferences well, achieving over 80% agreement, the same level of agreement between humans... limitations of LLM-as-a-judge, including position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases, as well as limited reasoning ability

claim: Self-preference bias in LLM judges is rooted in perplexity/familiarity: LLMs assign significantly higher scores to lower-perplexity outputs than human evaluators do, regardless of whether the output was self-generated.
quote: LLMs assign significantly higher evaluations to outputs with lower perplexity than human evaluators, regardless of whether the outputs were self-generated... the self-preference bias exists because LLMs prefer texts more familiar to them

claim: In pairwise code judging, swapping the presentation order of two responses can shift judge accuracy by over 10%, and expert-domain agreement between LLM judges and human SMEs runs only 60-68%.
quote: In pairwise code judging, simply swapping the presentation order of responses can lead to accuracy shifts exceeding 10%... agreement rates between LLM judges and human subject matter experts range from 60-68%

claim: A systematic 2026 study compared 9 debiasing strategies across 5 judges from 4 model families, 3 benchmarks, and 4 bias types, finding debiasing helps but the optimal strategy is model-dependent, with statistically significant gains of +7.2 to +11.2 points for select model-strategy pairs.
quote: statistically significant gains of +7.2 to +11.2 percentage points for select model-strategy pairs (after multiple testing correction)... 9 debiasing strategies were compared across 5 judges from 4 model families, 3 benchmarks, and 4 bias types

claim: Recommended mitigations for LLM-as-judge include calibrating against domain-specific human spot-checks, reference-guided grading where a correct answer exists, meta-judge over debate-style multi-model setups (which amplify bias), and using a judge from a different provider than the generator.
quote: calibrating your judge against human spot-checks for your specific domain; using reference-guided grading where a correct reference answer is available; using meta-judge approaches rather than debate-style multi-model setups, which amplify bias; and using a judge model from a different provider than your generator model

claim: As of June 2026 the SWE-bench Verified leaderboard (97 models) is led by Claude Mythos Preview at 93.9%, Claude Opus 4.8 at 88.6%, and Claude Opus 4.7 at 87.6%, with Gemini 3.1 Pro and DeepSeek-V4 clustered near 80.6%.
quote: Claude Mythos Preview (Anthropic): 0.939 ... Claude Opus 4.8: 0.886 ... Claude Opus 4.7: 0.876 ... Gemini 3.1 Pro and DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Max both achieved 0.806 ... evaluated 97 models ... last updated in June 2026

claim: SWE-bench Verified is a 500-issue human-validated subset of SWE-bench released August 13, 2024 by OpenAI with Princeton authors, after 93 developers reviewed tasks; 68.3% of original SWE-bench samples were filtered out for underspecification or unfair unit tests.
quote: 500 GitHub issues ... reviewed by 93 contracted software developers ... released on August 13, 2024 by OpenAI's Preparedness team ... 68.3% of SWE-bench samples were filtered out due to underspecification, unfair unit tests, or other issues

claim: SWE-bench Verified scores are increasingly inflated by contamination: models scoring 80%+ on Verified reach only about 46-57% on the contamination-resistant SWE-bench Pro, whose private codebases are legally inaccessible to model trainers.
quote: Models that score 80%+ on Verified only reach about 46-57% on Pro ... Because the private codebases are legally inaccessible to model trainers, contamination is structurally prevented on the Pro benchmark

claim: LiveCodeBench is a contamination-free code benchmark that continuously collects new problems from LeetCode, AtCoder and CodeForces, annotating each with a release date so models are scored only on problems released after their training cutoff, across code generation, self-repair, execution and test-output prediction.
quote: continuously collects new problems from programming contests (LeetCode, AtCoder, CodeForces) and evaluates four different scenarios: code generation, self-repair, code execution, and test output prediction. Problems are annotated with release dates to enable evaluation on unseen problems released after a model's training cutoff

claim: BigCodeBench comprises 1,140 practical programming tasks (with a harder ~150-task subset), testing both docstring-based completion and instruction-based generation, with models ranked by calibrated Pass@1 using greedy decoding.
quote: the full set of 1140 BigCodeBench tasks ... a subset of ~150 BigCodeBench tasks which is more user-facing and challenging ... Models are ranked according to (calibrated) Pass@1 using greedy decoding

claim: RepoBench (arXiv 2306.03091, June 2023) benchmarks repository-level code auto-completion via three interconnected tasks (Retrieval, Completion, Pipeline) for Python and Java, across cross-file-first, cross-file-random and in-file settings and context lengths from 2k to 16k tokens.
quote: three interconnected evaluation tasks: RepoBench-R (Retrieval), RepoBench-C (Code Completion), and RepoBench-P (Pipeline) ... three settings: cross-file-first, cross-file-random, and in-file ... five context length levels-2k, 4k, 8k, 12k, and 16k tokens

claim: Models score up to 76% identifying buggy file paths from issue text alone (no repo access), dropping below 53% on out-of-distribution repos; verbatim solution memorization ranged 11.7%-31.6% across models, indicating recall not reasoning.
quote: state-of-the-art (SoTA) models achieve up to 76% accuracy in identifying buggy file paths using only issue descriptions, without access to repository structure.

claim: SWE-rebench collects GitHub tasks post-dating model training cutoffs for decontaminated, timestamped evaluation; OpenAI's audit of 138 o3 failures found 59.4% were test-harness flaws and 32.67% of successful patches involved solution text leaking from the issue.
quote: 32.67% of successful patches involved solution leakage (solutions directly present in issue text or comments), and OpenAI's manual audit of 138 o3 failures revealed 59.4% were caused by test flaws

claim: Of 85 LLM-centric ICSE/ASE 2024 papers using OpenAI models, only 18 shared artifacts, only 5 were executable, and none could be fully reproduced (2 partial, 3 not reproducible).
quote: For none of the five studies, we were able to fully reproduce the results. Two studies seemed to be partially reproducible, and three studies did not seem to be reproducible.

claim: CR-Bench distinguishes raw bug-catch recall from real-world usefulness, using a signal-to-noise ratio as a proxy for developer trust because high recall with excess output causes developer fatigue and tool abandonment.
quote: A high SNR serves as a primary proxy for developer trust by quantifying the ratio of actionable signal to distracting hallucinations

claim: Benchmarks treating human PR comments as ground truth inherit noise: comments mix clarification questions, subjective style suggestions, and back-and-forth, and wording does not map cleanly to the underlying issue.
quote: Human review comments are often noisy artifacts of the review process: they may include clarification questions, subjective stylistic suggestions, or back-and-forth discussions between reviewers and authors

claim: A systematic review of LLM software-engineering benchmarks found nearly every benchmark had weaknesses in at least one dimension of construct validity, the degree to which a score supports claims about the target phenomenon.
quote: nearly every reviewed benchmark had weaknesses in at least one dimension of construct validity

claim: Best-Worst Scaling is more reliable than rating (Likert-style) scales: over 64K annotations split-half reliability was rho=0.98 for BWS vs 0.95 for rating scales (p<.001), and BWS matches the rating scale's 10N-annotation reliability with only 3N annotations.
quote: the average split-half reliability for BWS is rho=0.98 and for the rating scale method the reliability is rho=0.95 (the difference is statistically significant, p<.001)... matched by BWS with only 3N total annotations

claim: Independent peer-reviewed work beyond NLP (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications, 2019) confirms BWS improves measurement reliability over rating scales for social-perception/first-impressions data.
quote: Best-worst scaling improves measurement of first impressions

claim: For validating annotation rubrics, Krippendorff's alpha is preferred in NLP because it handles missing data, any number of annotators, and nominal/ordinal/interval data, whereas Cohen's kappa is limited to two annotators and Fleiss' kappa needs three or more raters with equal ratings per item; high IAA confirms consistency, not construct validity.
quote: High IAA only confirms that annotators are consistent, not that they are measuring the intended construct correctly.
